title: Case: Verdana Hotels
text: Verdana Hotels operates 35 mid-range hotels in Spain, Portugal and Italy with 4,200 employees. After the pandemic, demand is back, but the company struggles to staff kitchens and front desks. Staff turnover in housekeeping is 55 % a year, and 30 % of housekeepers are agency workers on short contracts. The CEO has announced a goal to become “the most sustainable hotel group in Southern Europe” by 2030.

Recruitment: hotel managers post jobs on generic job boards and hire mostly through personal recommendations of current staff. Interviews are informal; one manager says he looks for people “who look like they belong in a nice hotel”. Almost all front-desk staff are young and from the local majority population, while housekeeping is almost entirely migrant women.

Performance management: once a year, managers rate each employee on a 1–5 scale for “attitude” and “guest focus”. Hotel managers are ranked on monthly guest review scores and cost per occupied room; the bottom three managers lose their bonus. Several managers have cut housekeeping hours to improve cost per room.

Rewards: base pay follows the sector collective agreement. Front-desk staff receive a monthly bonus if their hotel's guest review score exceeds 8.5; housekeepers receive no variable pay. Pay is never discussed openly; new hires are asked about their previous salary.
